name: cardinality stated as design/capacity ('fixed-size, for a single entry', contrasted with 'allows multiple entries') counts vs only a content-count assertion ('contains exactly one entry') counts
side_a: No_deduct if the answer conveys the one-mapping limit in any form, including capacity/design framing ('fixed-size map designed for a single entry', 'allows only one entry') or an explicit contrast with HashMap's multi-entry capability, even if it never says the map 'contains' exactly one pair.
side_b: Deduct unless the answer asserts the actual content count of the singletonMap ('contains exactly one entry', 'has one key-value pair'); design/capacity phrasing such as 'fixed-size map designed for a single entry' or contrasting 'HashMap allows multiple entries' is treated as describing intent/structure rather than stating cardinality and is deducted.

name: Grounds the wrapping in this code's downstream use (messageParams needs a mutable map) vs. generic Map-class comparison only
side_a: No deduct if the answer explains WHY this particular call site wraps the singletonMap — i.e. names the consuming code (messageParams) and infers it needs/expects a mutable (HashMap) map.
side_b: Deduct if the answer only contrasts the two map types in the abstract (immutable one-entry vs. mutable resizable) without connecting the wrapping to the method that consumes the map in this snippet.

name: Accurate reading of the snippet (singletonMap wrapped in HashMap) vs. misstated/contradicted code behavior
side_a: No deduct if the answer correctly states the code builds a mutable HashMap *from* the immutable singletonMap and keeps its claims about the snippet consistent.
side_b: Deduct if the answer mischaracterizes the snippet — e.g. treats singletonMap as a not-taken alternative, misdescribes HashMap's implementation, or asserts the mutability is pointless/unused.

name: Ties the HashMap requirement to the specific `messageParams` parameter vs. speaks only about maps/APIs in general
side_a: Award credit when the answer explicitly identifies `messageParams` (the receiving method/parameter) as the thing that takes a HashMap — i.e., the requirement is attached to the actual declared parameter under discussion.
side_b: Deduct when the answer never names the consuming method and only compares HashMap vs singletonMap in the abstract, or attributes the need to unnamed 'APIs' / 'the code' — a generic mutability/implementation discussion does not identify the parameter requirement.

name: Asserts the HashMap parameter requirement vs. offers it as one speculative option among alternatives
side_a: Award credit when the answer asserts, without alternatives, that messageParams's parameter is/must be a HashMap.
side_b: Deduct when the HashMap-parameter claim is presented as a hedged guess or as one branch of a disjunction ('likely ... either requires X or expects a HashMap'), since the answer does not commit to the declared parameter type as the reason.

name: Definite verdict that the map is never altered vs. hedged speculation ('likely', 'either...or') that mutability might be needed
side_a: Do not deduct when the answer makes a definite, unhedged statement about what actually happens to the map in this code — e.g., that it is never altered/modified after being passed — even if the answer is brief and doesn't name call sites. A committed 'it isn't altered' verdict satisfies the read-only requirement.
side_b: Deduct when the answer only speculates about why a mutable map might be wanted — hedging with 'likely', 'probably', 'may', or offering a disjunction of possible reasons ('either the method modifies it or it expects a HashMap') — without ever committing to whether the map is actually read or written in messageParams. Hedged guessing leaves the read/write question unresolved and does not count as determining the usages are read-only.

name: Read-only usage identified vs. wrapping justified by a supposed mutable/HashMap API requirement
side_a: Do not deduct when the answer's account of why the copy exists still asserts the map itself is not written to in the actual code.
side_b: Deduct when the answer explains the wrapping by appeal to a generic API/type requirement — claiming the receiving method 'expects a HashMap type' or 'APIs that expect a mutable HashMap implementation' — since this substitutes a hypothetical signature constraint for any finding about how the map is used inside messageParams.
